nodes.title: Method: HistGradientBoosting with one-hot group plus permutation importance diagnostics
nodes.summary: Load the data and one-hot encode group, with median imputation for any missing values. Print summary statistics of y and the correlation of each feature with y. Fit HistGradientBoostingRegressor (seed from SEED) and run a small 5-fold CV grid over learning_rate {0.03, 0.1}, max_leaf_nodes {15, 31} and min_samples_leaf {10, 30}, with max_iter 1000 and early stopping. Print the CV RMSE for each setting. Refit the best setting on all of train. Compute permutation importance on a 20% holdout and print it for every feature. Then refit using only the features whose importance is clearly above zero, compare its CV RMSE, and use whichever variant has the lower CV RMSE to predict val and test.

nodes.title: Method: Spline GAM with group×x interactions, noise columns dropped
nodes.summary: Use only x1–x4 and a one-hot encoding of group. Build SplineTransformer features (n_knots 6, degree 3) for each x, plus pairwise products x_i*x_j, plus interactions of every group dummy with the raw x's and their spline bases. Fit RidgeCV with alphas on a log grid from 1e-3 to 1e3. Using 5-fold CV, compare four variants: (a) additive splines only, (b) + group intercepts, (c) + group×x interactions, (d) + pairwise x products. Also run variant (c) with noise1–noise6 added, to test whether they help. Print the CV RMSE of every variant and the largest coefficients. Predict val and test with the variant that has the best CV RMSE.

nodes.title: val rmse 0.5898 (+1.7472 vs baseline)
nodes.summary: Held-out test 0.5890 (never shown to agents).

details.analyst_analysis:
The headline result clearly beats the baseline, but the stated mechanism is mostly not what produced it. Validation RMSE was 0.5898, against a baseline of 2.3370 and a prediction of 1.7. That is a gain of 1.747, far above the 0.05 threshold. Cross-validation RMSE of the chosen variant was 0.6031 with a fold sd of 0.067, so validation agrees with CV and there is no sign of overfitting or leakage.

The ablation shows where the gain came from:
- Additive splines only (a): 2.396. This is about the same as the baseline, so smooth additive effects alone are no better than the trees.
- Adding group intercepts (b): 2.189. A modest gain.
- Adding group×x interactions (c): 2.372. This is worse than (b), and the fold sd rose from 0.33 to 0.55. In the additive setting the group×x terms add variance, not signal.
- Adding pairwise x products (d): 0.603. This cuts error by about 75%, and the top standardized coefficient is x2*x3 at +1.88, about 4× the next largest.

So y is not additive. The x2×x3 interaction dominates, with nonlinear x1 effects (spline coefficients about ±0.46) and smaller nonlinear x4 effects next. The group-specific x1 spline coefficients are similar across A, B and C (s(x1)_5 is about +0.22 in all three groups). That suggests a shared x1 shape rather than real group dependence.

The variants were cumulative, so (d) still contains the group×x terms. Whether they help once the pairwise products are present was not isolated. Dropping the noise columns is supported: adding noise1–6 to (c) changed RMSE by only +0.006. Overall, the hypothesis is supported in the sense that a structured basis model beats the trees, but its stated reasons (additive effects that depend on group) are refuted. The real driver is a multiplicative x2·x3 term.
analyst_lessons: An explicit x2*x3 product term is the main driver. Adding pairwise products cut CV RMSE from 2.37 to 0.60, and x2*x3 has a standardized coefficient of 1.88, about 4× any other term. Every future model should include x2*x3 explicitly.
y is not additive. Additive splines alone (2.40 CV) and the tree baseline (2.34) perform about the same, so both miss the interaction.

Group×x interactions hurt in the additive model: 2.19 → 2.37 CV, with fold sd rising 0.33 → 0.55. The group-specific x1 spline coefficients are nearly the same across A, B and C. Run an ablation of d without the group×x terms; it will likely match or beat 0.603 with far fewer than 149 features.
Group intercepts are worth about 0.2 RMSE (2.40 → 2.19) and should be kept.
noise1–6 carry no signal (+0.006 RMSE when added). Keep dropping them.
CV is reliable here: CV RMSE of 0.603 matched validation RMSE of 0.590. 5-fold CV can be used for model selection without spending validation.

Next steps: (1) remove pairs other than x2*x3 and the group×x terms to test a compact model of s(x1) + s(x4) + x2*x3 + group; (2) test whether x2·x3 is nonlinear, for example with a spline of the product or a tensor-product spline; (3) test group×(x2*x3); (4) give the trees an engineered x2*x3 feature, or ensemble them with the GAM, to reduce the remaining roughly 0.59 RMSE.

nodes.title: Method: Tensor-product spline in (x2,x3) + residual GBM structure check
nodes.summary: Drop noise columns for the main model. Base: per-variable splines on x1, x4 (n_knots 8) and group dummies. Interaction: the row-wise outer product of SplineTransformer(n_knots=6, degree=3) bases for x2 and x3 (about 64 columns), plus raw x2*x3. Fit RidgeCV (alphas logspace(-3,3,25)). Compare 5-fold CV against the same model with x2*x3 only in place of the tensor block. Then fit HistGradientBoosting (max_depth 3, 200 iters, lr 0.05) to out-of-fold residuals using ALL features (including noise1–6 and group codes). Print residual-model CV R² and permutation importances. If residual R² > 0.05, add the HGB residual correction (out-of-fold-validated) to the final predictions; otherwise use the better ridge model alone.

nodes.title: val rmse 0.8133 (+1.5237 vs baseline)
nodes.summary: Held-out test 0.7420 (never shown to agents).

details.analyst_analysis:
The tuned HistGradientBoosting model reached a validation RMSE of 0.8133. The baseline was 2.3370, so that is an improvement of 1.52, far above the 0.05 success threshold. It also beat the predicted 1.6. So the evidence supports the hypothesis as stated. However, it did not beat the best result before this experiment (0.5898). It is 0.22 RMSE worse, so it is not a new best.

Validation RMSE (0.8133) closely matches the CV RMSE of the selected model (0.8101), so CV is a reliable proxy here.

What the diagnostics showed:
1. **Nonlinear effects.** x2 and x3 have almost no linear correlation with y (-0.015 and +0.034). Yet they have the second- and third-highest permutation importance (1.49 and 1.51 RMSE increase, behind x1 at 2.25). Their effect on y is therefore strongly nonlinear or depends on interactions with other features, which linear correlation cannot see.
2. **Noise features.** All six noise columns have importance within about ±0.007, inside their standard errors, so they are pure noise. They also have about 5% missing values. Dropping them improved CV RMSE from 0.9334 to 0.8101 (-0.12). That is the largest single gain within this experiment.
3. **Regularisation.** Heavier regularisation helped consistently. min_samples_leaf=30 beat 10 in every pairing (by 0.13–0.19). 15 leaves beat 31 (by 0.07–0.13). Learning rate barely mattered (0.9334 vs 0.9427 at the best setting). The data has 1800 rows and the trees tend to overfit, so the optimum may lie beyond the grid (min_samples_leaf above 30, fewer leaves).
4. **Group** matters (importance 0.70), and so does x4 (0.58).

The remaining gap to the best result (0.59) suggests that piecewise-constant trees approximate a smooth or structured signal poorly. A model with explicit nonlinear or interaction terms in x2 and x3 would probably do better.
analyst_lessons: Drop noise1–noise6: their permutation importance is about 0 (|imp| ≤ 0.007) and removing them cut GBM CV RMSE from 0.933 to 0.810.

x2 and x3 have near-zero linear correlation with y (|r| < 0.04) but high permutation importance (about 1.5 each). Their effect is nonlinear or depends on interactions, so add explicit transforms such as x2*x3, x2^2, x3^2, sin/cos terms or splines, or check partial dependence and 2-D interaction plots.

On this data, boosted trees improve with stronger regularisation: min_samples_leaf=30 beat 10 by 0.13–0.19 RMSE, and 15 leaves beat 31. If trees are tried again, test min_samples_leaf of 50–100 and 7–15 leaves.
Learning rate (0.03 vs 0.1) made little difference (<0.01 RMSE) with early stopping, so it is not worth tuning further.
5-fold CV RMSE (0.810) matched validation RMSE (0.813), so CV can be trusted for model selection here.

Tree GBM with feature selection reached 0.813, still 0.22 worse than the best of 0.590. Next experiments should focus on structured or smooth models (feature-engineered linear models, GAMs or splines, group interactions) using only x1–x4 and group, rather than more tree tuning.

nodes.title: val rmse 0.5649 (+1.7721 vs baseline)
nodes.summary: Held-out test 0.5691 (never shown to agents).

details.analyst_analysis:
The hypothesis was that a simple GAM (additive splines on x1–x4, plus raw x2*x3, plus group intercepts) would match or beat 0.59 with far fewer features than #3's 149. Validation RMSE was 0.5649, close to the predicted 0.57 and 0.025 better than the previous best of 0.5898. That gain over the previous best is below the 0.05 threshold. The 'success' label comes from the 1.77 improvement over the 2.337 baseline. The model has 44 features, not about 30: the splines produce 40 columns (10 per variable) instead of the expected roughly 26, but this is still about 3.4 times fewer than #3.

What each part did:
(1) Group intercepts matter most. Adding them to splines plus x2*x3 cut CV RMSE from 1.170 to 0.545 (R2 from 0.873 to 0.972). The group effects are roughly A -0.13, B +1.31, C -1.15 on the raw scale.
(2) The other five pairwise products add nothing. CV RMSE was 0.5463 vs 0.5448, all their raw coefficients are 0.043 or smaller, and the x2*x3 coefficient did not move (1.974).
(3) Letting the x2*x3 slope vary by group adds nothing. CV RMSE was identical (0.5448, sd 0.027). The group-specific slopes came out nearly equal (1.008, 0.980, 1.001), and ridge simply split the roughly 2.0 total slope between the shared and per-group terms. This means the slope is the same in every group, about 1.97.
(4) CV RMSE for variant b (0.545 ± 0.026) is consistent with validation RMSE (0.565), so there is no sign of overfitting.
The likely true model is additive smooth effects plus about 1.97·x2·x3 plus a group shift. The remaining error, about 0.55, may be close to the noise floor.
analyst_lessons: Group intercepts are the most important term: CV RMSE drops from 1.17 to 0.545 when they are added, so every model should include them.
x2*x3 is the only interaction that matters (raw coefficient about 1.97, stable across variants). The other pairwise products have coefficients of 0.043 or smaller and do not improve CV, so drop them.
Group-specific x2*x3 slopes come out nearly equal (about 1.0 each when split with the shared term) and CV is unchanged, so the slope does not depend on group. Do not add group×x terms.
44 features (splines with 8 knots and degree 3 make 10 columns per variable, plus x2*x3 and group dummies) beat 149 features (0.565 vs 0.590 validation RMSE). Fewer features generalized better here.

CV RMSE of 0.545 ± 0.026 versus 0.565 on validation suggests the remaining error is close to irreducible noise. Further gains are likely to be smaller than the 0.05 threshold. Cheap remaining checks: tune the number of spline knots and per-feature smoothing, or test whether any x1–x4 spline is actually linear.
Gain over the previous best (0.025) was below the 0.05 threshold, so judge future experiments against the best result so far, not the 2.337 baseline.

nodes.title: val rmse 0.5308 (+1.8062 vs baseline)
nodes.summary: Held-out test 0.5592 (never shown to agents).

details.analyst_analysis:
The score improved, but not for the reason the hypothesis gave. Validation RMSE was 0.5308, against 0.5898 before this run and a baseline of 2.337, so the deterministic outcome counts as a success.

The hypothesis said a tensor-product spline in (x2,x3) would capture a curved interaction, and that idea failed:
- **Tensor block:** 5-fold CV RMSE 4.80 (R² −1.13), which is +4.26 worse than the bilinear version.
- **Bilinear version:** splines on x1 and x4 (n_knots 8), group dummies and a raw x2·x3 term, with noise columns dropped. It reached CV RMSE 0.5389 (R² 0.973) and is the model that was kept (alpha 3.16).

An R² of −1.1 for a ridge-penalised basis of about 64 columns is not a modelling result. It points to a pipeline or extrapolation bug, for example spline bases blowing up at the edges of a fold, unscaled outer products, or columns misaligned in the row-wise product. So the tensor arm doesn't really test curvature.

The residual check gives independent evidence against curvature. A boosted model fitted to the out-of-fold residuals on all features reached only R² 0.020, below the 0.05 threshold. Permutation importance for x2 was +0.012 and for x3 −0.004, so no meaningful x2–x3 structure is left after the bilinear term. Noise columns were about zero (−0.008 to +0.008). The one notable signal is x4 at +0.12 importance, which may mean the x4 spline is underfit. Adding the boosted correction gave a small gain (0.5335 vs 0.5389 CV) but was not used because of the threshold.

Most likely, the gain over 0.5898 comes from the spline base terms and/or dropping the noise columns, not from any form of the interaction. This run doesn't separate those two factors.
analyst_lessons: The current best model is: splines on x1 and x4 (n_knots 8), group dummies and a raw x2*x3 term, fitted with RidgeCV and noise columns dropped. It gives CV RMSE 0.539 and validation 0.531.

A bilinear x2*x3 term looks sufficient: after it, a boosted model on the residuals finds R² of only 0.02, with x2 and x3 permutation importances at or below 0.012. Further work on curved x2–x3 interactions is unlikely to pay off.

The tensor-spline block scored CV R² −1.13, which signals a bug or extrapolation problem, not a real result. Check the scale of the basis, the edge extrapolation settings and per-fold sanity before trusting high-dimensional basis expansions.
x4 is the only residual feature with real permutation importance (+0.12 R² drop). Next, try more knots or a different basis for x4, or x4 interactions (e.g. x4*group).
Noise columns noise1–6 add no residual signal (importances between −0.008 and +0.008). Keep them excluded.
Adding the boosted residual correction improved CV RMSE by only about 0.005 (0.5389 to 0.5335). The remaining error is close to the noise floor, so expect diminishing returns below about 0.53.

nodes.title: Method: Per-feature ablation and smoothness tuning of the parsimonious GAM
nodes.summary: Features: x1–x4 and one-hot group; drop the noise columns. Base model = the #4 variant (b): per-feature SplineTransformer + raw x2*x3 + group dummies, fitted with RidgeCV(alphas=logspace(-4,3,30)). Use repeated 5-fold CV (3 repeats, seeded from SEED). (1) Leave-one-out ablation: remove the term for each of x1, x2, x3, x4 (keeping x2*x3) and report the change in CV. (2) For each feature, choose among {drop, linear, spline with n_knots 4, 6, 10, 15} by coordinate descent: 2 passes, accepting a change only if CV improves by more than 0.003. (3) Print the selected configuration, its CV mean and sd, and the fitted partial effect of each spline evaluated at 9 quantiles. (4) Check robustness: refit the selected configuration with HuberRegressor on the same design and report its CV. Use whichever of Ridge and Huber has the lower CV to refit on all of train and predict val and test.

nodes.title: Method: ARD Gaussian process on GAM residuals to find leftover interactions
nodes.summary: Fit the #4 variant (b) model (splines with 8 knots on x1–x4 + x2*x3 + group dummies, RidgeCV) and compute out-of-fold residuals with 5-fold CV. Standardize x1–x4 and append group dummies scaled by 0.5. Fit a sklearn GaussianProcessRegressor on the residuals with kernel ConstantKernel*RBF(length_scale=[1]*n_features, bounds (1e-2, 1e3)) + WhiteKernel, normalize_y=True, n_restarts_optimizer=1, random_state=SEED. To keep the time limit, optimize the hyperparameters on a random subsample of 1000 rows, then refit on all rows with the kernel fixed (optimizer=None). Print the learned length-scales, where large means irrelevant, and print sqrt(WhiteKernel noise) mapped back to y units. Compute the 5-fold CV RMSE of GAM + GP-residual predictions, using fixed kernel hyperparameters inside the folds, and compare it with the GAM alone. Predict val and test with GAM + GP if CV improves by more than 0.01; otherwise use the GAM alone. Print the elapsed time.

nodes.title: val rmse 0.5242 (+1.8127 vs baseline)
nodes.summary: Held-out test 0.5419 (never shown to agents).

details.analyst_analysis:
The hypothesis is supported, but the gain is small. Validation RMSE was 0.5242. That is 0.0066 better than the previous best (0.5308) and better than the predicted 0.55. It clears the success threshold easily against the 2.337 baseline. Most of that margin was already won by experiment #4, so the extra gain from tuning is marginal.

In cross-validation, the tuned model scored 0.5311 ± 0.0212, down from 0.5463 ± 0.0221 for the uniform 8-knot base model. The 0.015 drop is smaller than one CV standard deviation. The improvement also showed up on the validation set, though, so it probably did not come from overfitting the selection procedure.

**What drives y (from the ablation):**
- **x1 is the dominant term.** Dropping it raised CV RMSE by 1.69.
- **x4 is the second most important.** Dropping it raised CV RMSE by 0.58.
- **x2 and x3 add nothing on their own** once the x2*x3 product is in the model. Dropping either one slightly improved CV (by 0.003 and 0.004).

**The selected model** is: x1 with an 8-knot spline, x2 and x3 dropped (their product kept), x4 with a 10-knot spline, plus the group dummies, fitted with Ridge (alpha 3.86).

**What the fitted effects look like:**
- **x1 looks like one period of a sine wave** with amplitude about 2.9. It bottoms out near -2.9 at x1 ≈ -1.3, rises to about +2.9 at x1 ≈ 1.4, and falls back to about 1.3 at 2.7.
- **x4 looks like a step function.** It sits flat near -1.0 for x4 below about 0.4 and flat near +1.0 above about 0.6, with a jump between 0.48 and 0.60. The spline wobbles around the jump: it dips to -1.054 at x4 = 0.38, then 1.175 at 0.60 falls back to 0.941 at 0.71. That wobble suggests a smooth spline is a poor fit for a sharp jump.

**Robustness check:** HuberRegressor did not help (CV 0.5321 vs 0.5311 for Ridge), so the noise does not look heavy-tailed. The remaining error of about 0.52–0.53 may be close to the noise floor. The step in x4 is the most likely place left to gain.
analyst_lessons: In the GAM, the x2 and x3 main-effect terms are redundant once x2*x3 is included. Dropping both improved CV from 0.5463 to 0.5393. Keep only the product.
Feature importance from the ablation: x1 is dominant (dropping it adds 1.69 CV RMSE) and x4 is second (adds 0.58). The group dummies remain in the model.
x1's effect looks like a sine wave with amplitude about 2.9 (minimum near x1 = -1.3, maximum near 1.4). A parametric sin/cos basis is worth trying in place of the spline.

x4's effect looks like a step from about -1 to +1, with the jump between 0.48 and 0.60, and the 10-knot spline wobbles around it. Next, try a threshold indicator 1[x4 > c] with c tuned somewhere in 0.48–0.60, possibly plus a light spline.
Huber gave no gain over Ridge (0.5321 vs 0.5311), so heavy-tailed noise is not the issue. Don't spend more effort on robust losses.

Remaining gains look small: tuning improved validation by only 0.0066 over the previous best, and the CV change (0.015) was smaller than the CV standard deviation (about 0.021). Treat 0.52 as close to the floor unless the x4 step is modeled more sharply.
Choosing spline smoothness per feature by coordinate descent ran fast (about 18 s) and converged within 2 passes. It is a cheap template for future structure searches.

nodes.title: val rmse 0.5453 (+1.7917 vs baseline)
nodes.summary: Held-out test 0.5416 (never shown to agents).

details.analyst_analysis:
Validation RMSE was 0.5453, which is +1.79 better than the 2.337 baseline. But it is 0.0145 worse than the previous best (0.5308), and the CV gain did not carry over to validation.

**CV vs validation**
- In 5-fold CV the GAM plus GP-on-residuals scored 0.5275, against 0.5451 for the GAM alone (gain 0.0176). That passed the 0.01 gate, so the GP was used for the final predictions.
- On validation the GAM+GP scored 0.5453. That is about the same as the GAM's out-of-fold score (0.5466) and well above the 0.5275 CV figure.
- The CV is optimistic. The kernel hyperparameters were tuned on 1000 rows of the full out-of-fold residuals and then held fixed inside the folds, so the tuning had already seen every fold's targets.

**What the learned kernel shows**
- Length-scales are on standardized inputs; large means the feature doesn't matter. x2 (1e3), x1 (148) and g=C (841) are effectively irrelevant. x3 (2.23) is weakly relevant.
- Signal is concentrated in x4 (0.045) and the group-B dummy (0.0375). The group-A dummy is at 0.496.
- An x4 length-scale of 0.045 standard deviations is extremely short for 1800 rows. That looks more like fitting noise than a smooth leftover x4 or group-B interaction.
- The GP signal variance is only 0.125 of the normalized residual variance, and the WhiteKernel accounts for 0.871. So the residuals are about 87% noise.

**Noise floor**
The estimated noise is 0.507 in y units. The current best (0.531) is within about 0.024 of that, so little reducible error is left. That estimate is the most reliable result here.

The hypothesis was that the GP would recover leftover interactions that improve predictions. That isn't confirmed: the gain on validation is null, or negative relative to the best model, while the diagnostics point to a possible x4 × group-B effect. Runtime was 28 s.
analyst_lessons: The noise floor estimated from the GP's WhiteKernel is about 0.507 RMSE in y units. The best score so far, 0.531, is only about 0.024 above it, so expect future gains of 0.02 or less.

Tuning GP hyperparameters on all out-of-fold residuals and then fixing them inside the CV folds leaks information: CV said 0.5275 but validation gave 0.5453. Tune the kernel inside each fold, or hold out data that the tuning never sees.

The GP ignored x1, x2 and group C (length-scales above 100) and concentrated on x4 (0.045) and the group-B dummy (0.0375). If anything is left to find, test an explicit x4-by-group-B spline interaction in the GAM rather than a GP.
The GP explained only about 12.5% of the residual variance, so a general nonparametric model on the residuals adds little over GAM + x2*x3 + group effects.
The GAM+GP model (0.5453 on validation) did worse than the earlier best (0.5308), so keep the earlier best as the incumbent model.
